content: All included studies utilized either cross-sectional or case-control designs. The risk of bias in patient selection, index tests, or reference standards was evaluated using the QUADAS-2 tool. Among the studies reviewed, 21 were identified as having at least one category with a high risk of bias. Bias in patient selection often stemmed from inadequate descriptions of the selection process and clinical scenarios. Bias in the index test was primarily due to the absence of blinding during the interpretation of test results. Bias in the reference standard arose from the use of multiple reference standards, such as enzyme immunoassays (EIA), nucleic acid testing (NAT), and/or immunoblot assays. Bias in the flow and timing of studies was mainly attributed to insufficiently reported details. The quality of the included studies was assessed using QUADAS-2, which evaluated bias and concerns regarding applicability across domains such as patient selection, index tests, reference standards, and flow/timing. For example, studies like Al-Tahish et al. (2013) and Bonacini et al. (2001) demonstrated varying levels of risk, with some studies showing high risk (HR) in specific domains, while others had low risk (LR) or unclear risk (UC). The diagnostic accuracy of the included studies was derived from 127 data points across 52 studies, encompassing 52,273 unique test measurements. Some studies contributed additional data points by comparing the accuracy of multiple tests, reporting results from different study sites, or evaluating tests across various specimen types. Sample sizes ranged from 37 to 17,894 participants. Sensitivity and specificity estimates for HCV antibody (HCV Ab) tests were visualized in Figure 2, which highlighted the performance of these tests across the studies. Thirty-two studies evaluated the accuracy of 30 different rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), with the OraQuick ADVANCE® test from OraSure Technologies being the most commonly assessed. Other tests included an Ag-Ab test by Bio-Rad and a combination HIV-HCV test by MedMira. Pooled test accuracy for RDTs compared to EIA alone was evaluated in five studies, involving a total sample size of 15,943. The pooled sensitivity and specificity of RDTs were comparable to those of EIAs, although some inconsistency in sensitivity was observed due to variability among the included tests. Thirteen studies compared RDTs to NAT or immunoblot reference standards, with a total sample size of 6,683. Similarly, 14 studies evaluated RDTs against combined EIA, NAT, and/or immunoblot standards, involving 42,212 samples. Twelve studies compared the accuracy of EIAs using oral fluid samples to blood samples, with a total sample size of 14,546. The pooled accuracy of oral HCV Ab RDTs compared to blood-based reference standards was also assessed, with 12 studies contributing data. Forty-five studies used blood samples for evaluations, with a total sample size of 89,608. Eight studies specifically reported the sensitivity and specificity of the OraQuick test, involving 9,024 samples. Six studies evaluated three other brands of oral kits, with a total sample size of 6,652. The performance of oral RDTs was found to be slightly less accurate than blood-based RDTs but may be more practical in certain settings, such as among individuals with difficult venous access. The review highlighted the advantages and disadvantages of laboratory-based EIAs versus RDTs. EIAs are highly accurate, automated, and capable of high throughput but require laboratory facilities, specialized equipment, and trained personnel. In contrast, RDTs are accessible at lower levels of the healthcare system, can use non-invasive specimens, and provide rapid results, enabling same-visit treatment initiation. However, RDTs are less accurate than EIAs, rely on subjective interpretation, and lack built-in quality control. The review also identified methodological challenges in evaluating diagnostic accuracy. All included studies used cross-sectional or case-control designs, which introduced potential bias. The use of diverse reference standards complicated the pooling of performance data. Most studies employed convenience sampling, and panel studies were excluded to ensure clinical relevance. Further research is needed to understand the performance of HCV Ab tests among co-infected individuals and to address the variability in diagnostic accuracy across different RDT brands. In conclusion, while HCV Ab RDTs, including those using oral fluid, demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity, their performance varied widely across brands and settings. Policymakers and healthcare practitioners must carefully consider the trade-offs between cost, accuracy, and accessibility when selecting diagnostic tests for HCV screening. The deployment of specific tests should align with the healthcare infrastructure, disease prevalence, and population needs, ensuring that the chosen strategy maximizes the identification of HCV cases while remaining cost-effective.
